content: The work was conducted for 41 members, with interests declared or identified. The following actions were taken: 1. Nomination to the US Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee: The individual was nominated by representatives from various organizations, including the North American Branch of the International Life Sciences Institute, the American Beverage Association, the American Bakers Association, the Grain Chain, the Grocery Manufacturers Association, the USA Dry Pea & Lentil Council, and the American Pulse Association. 2. Honorariums for Presentations: The individual received honorariums for delivering presentations on the development process of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans and food labeling policies in the United States. These presentations were given at scientific meetings organized by PMK Associates (including the Institute of Food Technologists and the American Oil Chemists’ Society), the McCormick Science Institute, the Fibre Association Japan, and the Mushroom Council. 3. Membership in the International Food Information Council (IFIC): The individual served as a member of the Board of Trustees for IFIC in 2021. This role ensured that IFIC upheld its responsibilities as a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization. 4. Role in the International Life Sciences Institute North America: The individual acted as a government liaison, evaluated research, and organized webinars on the microbiome in 2018. 5. Webinar Presentation for the International Dairy Foods Association: In 2020, the individual presented a webinar on the work of the 2020 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee. No remuneration was received for this activity, and it was not considered a conflict of interest due to the individual’s role as a national authority. 6. Nomination to the US Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee by Industry Groups: There was no relationship or affiliation between the nominator and the nominee. None of the declared interests were directly relevant to the guideline's objective or represented a conflict of interest. It was concluded that these interests would not impact the individual’s ability to serve objectively as a member of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health. 7. Participation in the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health: The individual was allowed to fully participate as a member of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health throughout the guideline development process. 8. Declaration of Interests by Other Members: No other members of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health declared any interests, nor were any independently identified. External Peer Review Group: 1. Amos Laar: Received research support from the International Development Research Center, Canada, for studying the food environments of Ghanaian children to prevent obesity and non-communicable diseases (MEALS4NCDs). This funding was not considered a conflict of interest for serving as an external reviewer of the guideline. 2. Allison Sylvetsky: Participated in a speaking engagement in 2019 for Siggi’s sessions, an educational portal hosted by Siggi’s Icelandic Yogurt Company. The presentation, titled “Sweeteners, weight, and health: the state of the science,” involved a small honorarium. This was not considered a conflict of interest for serving as an external reviewer of the guideline. 3. Mathilde Touvier: Received research funding from public institutions (European Research Council, French National Cancer Institute, French Ministry of Health) for projects on food additives, including artificial sweeteners, and health. This funding was not considered a conflict of interest for serving as an external reviewer of the guideline. No other members of the external peer review group declared any interests, nor were any independently identified. Systematic Review Teams: No members of the systematic review teams declared any interests, nor were any independently identified. Key Questions in PICO Format: 1. What is the effect of higher intake of non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) compared with lower intake on prioritized health outcomes in adults, children, and pregnant women? 2. What is the effect of replacing free sugars with NSS on prioritized health outcomes in adults, children, and pregnant women? The population of interest includes apparently healthy adults and children in low-, middle-, and high-income countries, including those with elevated BMI. Population characteristics such as age, gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and health background were considered. GRADE Evidence Profiles: 1. The evidence on the effects of NSS intake was assessed using GRADE methodology. The certainty of evidence was generally low to very low due to limitations in study design, risk of bias, and heterogeneity. 2. Most randomized controlled trials (RCTs) included in the meta-analyses for body fatness measures had unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting of methods. 3. Less than half of the trials for body weight and slightly more than half for BMI used appropriate randomization methods. Allocation concealment was adequately reported in less than a quarter of the trials. 4. Blinding of participants was only possible in a few studies, and many trials did not report sufficient details to assess blinding of outcome assessment. 5. Participant dropout rates were significant in about half of the trials, raising concerns about attrition bias. Summary of Findings: 1. The effects of NSS on health outcomes were small and likely of little to no clinical significance. 2. Behavioral responses to NSS may differ between populations habituated to sweet-tasting foods and those with limited exposure to such foods. 3. Intermediate markers such as blood lipids, glycemic markers, and blood pressure were prioritized in the outcomes of interest but are not validated surrogates for disease. 4. The WHO NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health did not downgrade outcomes for indirectness, as intermediate markers were considered informative. Limitations: 1. Many trials lacked sufficient detail in reporting methods, creating uncertainty regarding the risk of bias. 2. Funnel plot analyses suggested a slight possibility of publication bias, but this was not of significant concern. 3. The majority of trials had adequate randomization, but allocation concealment and blinding were often unclear or inadequate. In conclusion, while the evidence on NSS was assessed as low to very low certainty, the findings provide some insights into their effects on health outcomes. However, methodological limitations and heterogeneity across studies highlight the need for more rigorous research in this area.
